rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
notice period before filing complaint for dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds
The Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 section 138 notice demand payment
The Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 section 142 cognizance of offences
rows.answer:
A demand for payment by giving a notice in writing must be made within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. The drawer of the cheque then has fifteen days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment, as stated in the Supreme Court judgment in "Kamlesh Kumar versus State of Bihar & Anr." [1] citing Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The written notice demanding payment must be given within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The drawer of the cheque must fail to make the payment within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to consideration under negotiable instruments
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
rows.answer:
Until the contrary is proved, every negotiable instrument is presumed to have been made or drawn for consideration, and every such instrument, when accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred, is presumed to have been accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. Furthermore, it is presumed that the holder of a cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [4]. In a dispute between an endorser of a negotiable warehouse receipt and his endorsee, unless proved otherwise, it is presumed that the endorsement has been made for full consideration, under Section 22 of The Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act, 2007 [6].

As shown in the Supreme Court judgment in "K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr.", the presumption is one of law and imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption that the negotiable instrument was made for consideration, which throws the burden of proof of failure of consideration on the maker of the promissory note [11].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to an agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, the contract is not voidable if consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence, and the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as stated in the exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Additionally, a misrepresentation or fraud that did not cause the consent of the party on whom it was practised does not render the contract voidable, according to the explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 mental capacity soundness of mind for contract
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 covers what agreements are contracts, requiring them to be made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object [6].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder causing death with intention
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
Indian Penal Code section 302 murder
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, previously Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) [1][7]. In State through Superintendent of Police, CBI/SIT etc. versus Nalini and Ors. etc. etc., the Supreme Court excerpt quotes this punishment provision for murder [11]. In Bharatkumar Rameshchandra Barot versus State of Gujarat, the Supreme Court upheld the enhancement of sentence to life imprisonment under Section 302 of the IPC [7].

Related provisions:
- Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which covers punishment for murder by life-convict, providing for death or imprisonment for life meaning the remainder of that person's natural life [5].
- Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which covers punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder [3].

The old law this replaced: section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder) [9].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
punishment for theft Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft punishment
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) [1][8]. 

In case of a second or subsequent conviction under this section, the punishment shall be rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and extending up to five years, along with fine, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

For a first-time conviction of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, upon the return of the value of the property or restoration of the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft in a dwelling house, means of transport, place of worship, or of government/local authority property, punishing it with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [5].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

rows.answer:
A person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail when arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or when appearing or brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, provided there are no reasonable grounds for believing the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and the person is not barred by previous conviction rules [1]. (This current law is Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, previously Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) [1][3]. In Gurcharan Singh & Ors. versus State (Delhi Administration), the Supreme Court noted that if there appear to be reasonable grounds to believe the accused has committed an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, a ban is imposed against granting bail, whereas in all other non-bailable cases judicial discretion will be exercised in favour of granting bail subject to conditions [11].

rows.question: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
queries: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
application for setting aside arbitral award grounds limitation period
The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 section 34 application for setting aside arbitral award

topSources: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 s34

rows.answer:
An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only if the party making the application establishes on the basis of the record of the arbitral tribunal that a party was under some incapacity, the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it or under the law for the time being in force, the party was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present its case, the award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of submission, or the composition of the arbitral tribunal or arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties or Part I of the Act, under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1]. As discussed by the Supreme Court in BATLIBOI ENVIRONMENTAL ENGINEERS LIMITED versus HINDUSTAN PETROLEUM CORPORATION LIMITED AND ANOTHER, sub-section (2) to Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 stipulates grounds on which a court may set aside an arbitral award [1].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s58
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s69
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s123
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54
rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, according to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [5]. 

To constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another, meaning all rights and interests in the property possessed by a person are transferred with free consent to another person for a price called consideration, as discussed in the Supreme Court judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others [11].

Regarding completion and transfer of title, the conveyance has to be regarded in accordance with law so that the transaction of sale is complete and title passes from the seller to the buyer without the transferor retaining any part of their interest or right, as stated in the Supreme Court judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others [11].

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
queries: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
rows.answer:
The punishment for identity theft using a computer or communication device by personating is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to one lakh rupees under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [4].

Related provisions:

rows.question: What is theft punishment?
queries: What is theft punishment?
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
rows.answer:
The punishment for theft under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or fine, or both [5][10]. For a second or subsequent conviction under this section, the punishment is rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and up to five years, along with a fine [5]. In cases of first-time conviction where the stolen property is worth less than five thousand rupees, the punishment upon return or restoration of the property's value or the stolen property itself is community service [5].
